journal_feed.title: Rating an Experience Makes People Notice How It Is Changing: Consequences for Hedonic Adaptation and Consumer Enjoyment
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Repeated measurement is common in both marketing research and practice. For example, experimenters often ask participants to evaluate multiple similar products, and service providers regularly check in to see how customers are doing. Such practices rest on the assumption that collecting more data simply reveals consumers’ experiences and preferences as they evolve over time. The present research finds that repeated measurement also shapes them. Specifically, repeatedly probing consumers about an experience draws attention to how it is changing, prompting consumers to notice incremental differences more than if they were probed less or simply left alone. This process has important consequences for hedonic adaptation and enjoyment. In contexts of negative change, repeated ratings exacerbate adaptation by making incremental declines more salient, accelerating boredom and disengagement. In contexts of positive change, repeated ratings enhance experiences by making incremental improvements more salient. Eight studies (plus eight supplemental replications; total N = 16,311), spanning diverse hedonic stimuli (including games, foods, songs, videos, and artwork) and methodological approaches (including mediation and moderation), highlight this core idea that change is amplified when ratings draw attention to it. The research discusses how repeated measurement may thereby distort understandings of hedonic decline and consumer preferences, and how to harness these insights to promote longer-lasting consumer enjoyment.

journal_feed.title: Brand-Neutral Content Marketing and Endogenous Search Prominence
journal_feed.abstract: Brand-neutral content marketing attracts consumers by addressing category-level needs without directly promoting the brand. Although this may position a firm as consumers’ first point of inquiry, it leaves consumers only partially informed about brand fit. Rivals can exploit this gap by providing brand-specific information. Using a game-theoretic framework, we examine when content marketing generates endogenous search prominence and how the resulting search dynamics shape competitive communication strategies. We show that content marketing can provide a counterintuitive competitive edge: by shaping the information structure of consumer search, it influences rival pricing incentives, giving rise to asymmetric communication equilibria sustained by an information–exploitation tradeoff that governs profit allocation between the prominent gatekeeper and the non-prominent follower. When prices cannot be credibly committed, exploitation permanently dominates and content marketing becomes the unique equilibrium strategy. Brand strength and appeal breadth further determine which firm adopts content marketing.

journal_feed.title: Growing sentimental value through object usage
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers often protect their sentimentally valuable possessions by storing them away, which precludes them from being used. Across five studies, we show that usage of sentimentally valuable objects increases their sentimental value. Process evidence suggests one reason this happens: Repeatedly using a sentimentally valuable object makes the association held by the object (i.e., the source of its sentimental value) salient more frequently. This leads one to believe that such an association is more closely integrated into their self‐concept, which cyclically enhances the sentimental value of the object. We conclude by discussing the contribution of these findings to the literature, providing recommendations to marketers and consumers, and elaborating on directions for future research.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Double-Edged Offline Touchpoint: How Self-Pickup Stations Reshape Pure-Play E-Commerce Transactions
journal_feed.abstract: Click-and-collect services through self-pickup stations have gained popularity as an alternative to traditional home delivery in e-commerce. This fulfillment option can increase customer purchases by enhancing post-purchase convenience and reducing transaction costs. However, increased hassle costs for customers and exposure to offline competition make the net impact uncertain. This study utilizes a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) approach to analyze individual-level transaction data from an online shopping platform in Asia. Self-pickup station openings are found to have a positive net effect on customer spending and shopping frequency on the platform, without cannibalizing home delivery. A closer examination of customer dynamics reveals that station openings stabilize the platform’s user base by reducing customer churn and deepening engagement among existing shoppers, rather than driving new user acquisition. Furthermore, these positive effects are moderated by: station accessibility, level of nearby offline competition, and product attributes. Specifically, this paper provides the first empirical evidence that the positive effect of pickup stations can be reduced, if platforms locate them close to major offline retail alternatives. These findings provide important implications for e-commerce platforms regarding self-pickup station benefits, product suitability, and location strategy to reduce the risk of customer loss to offline retailers.

journal_feed.title: Multi-stakeholder market shaping for sustainability: effort types and enactment pathways in B2B markets
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Marketing scholarship has primarily focused on influencing consumer behavior towards sustainability, yet many sustainability challenges require market-level changes across multiple stakeholders. Addressing this gap, we examine how heterogeneous stakeholders collectively shape markets for sustainability. We conduct a multi-case study of B2B markets whose impact on climate change and biodiversity is actively contested. Drawing on institutional field theory, we conceptualize market shaping for sustainability as linked to issue fields where diverse stakeholders engage to influence market trajectories. Our abductive analysis identifies four types of multi-stakeholder market-shaping efforts pursuing markedly different—at times opposing—market-level outcomes: status quo maintenance, targeted reform, infrastructure reform, and market contraction. To explain this variation, we delineate four pathways through which stakeholders enact sustainability-related issues—two for challengers and two for incumbents. By linking these pathways to intended market-level outcomes, we advance theory on market-based sustainability interventions and offer actionable insights for navigating multi-stakeholder market-shaping processes.

journal_feed.title: Thank You, Now What? How Donors Respond to Calls to Action
journal_feed.abstract: We study whether thank-you communications that charities send to past donors should include a call to action and show that the answer depends on whether the donor has already given in the current giving cycle.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
journal_feed.abstract: Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

journal_feed.title: Through thick and thin? When sustainable packaging design increases consumer waste generation
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Packaging decisions involve a complex balance of cost, functionality, efficiency, branding, and sustainability initiatives. One promising sustainability strategy that also reduces costs is lightweighting, a manufacturing practice aimed at reducing raw material usage. In reducing raw material use, lightweighting results in structural changes to the packaging, specifically a reduction in packaging density, which has downstream consequences on consumer disposal. When assessing packaging for disposability cues, we show packaging density drives perceptions of its quality, value, and associated feelings of waste aversion. While lightweighting reduces firms’ waste, this work finds that once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging. However, prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness. This work highlights that even sustainable firm practices can result in unintended and unsustainable consequences.

journal_feed.title: Returnless Partial Refunds: A Large-Scale Field Experiment in E-Commerce
journal_feed.abstract: A large-scale field experiment shows AI-enabled returnless partial refunds increase customer value and reduce operating costs while raising strategic-behavior risks.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Infinite-Scrolling vs. Pagination: The Impact of Interface Layouts on Product Returns
journal_feed.abstract: Interface layout, although a fundamental and prominent aspect inherent to online interfaces, has received limited attention in consumer research. This paper explores how the two major types of interface layout (infinite scrolling and pagination) influence consumers’ product return behavior in the context of free returns, a standard policy on e-commerce sites. Across five studies featuring real websites, we show that an infinite-scrolling (versus paginated) layout increases consumers’ tendency to return purchased products. This effect occurs because infinite scrolling dampens consumers’ perceived navigational control over the website, which impairs their choice closure after making decisions, thereby increasing product return intentions. We also identify both theoretically relevant and managerially important moderators and interventions to mitigate this adverse effect of infinite scrolling, such as incorporating navigational aids (e.g., displaying sequence numbers alongside), providing affirmative feedback, and accounting for the cost of product returns. This research not only contributes to the literature on interface effects, website navigation, and product returns but also provides applied insights for marketing practitioners.

journal_feed.title: Pathways to premium: How habits and benefits shape conversion and retention in freemium subscription models
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Numerous digital services rely on freemium models, yet the mechanisms that move users from free usage to premium subscriptions remain poorly understood. This research examines how expected benefits of premium access, experienced benefits during trials, and habit development in free and premium contexts jointly shape conversion and retention. Across four empirical field studies in a freemium subscription setting, we show that habits in the free version are double‑edged: they can increase conversion by reinforcing expected benefits of the premium version, yet also anchor users in continued free usage through inertia. Habits formed while using the premium version, together with experienced premium benefits, generally support paid conversion and long‑term retention. In discounted trial settings, we further identify an inverse‑U‑shaped relationship between premium‑side habits and retention, with very strong habits associated with lower retention than moderate levels. These insights inform the design of effective freemium and trial strategies.

journal_feed.title: From liability to asset: How campaign context determines whether body weight helps or hurts online fundraisers
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Political Extremism and Post-Purchase Customer–Brand Relationships
journal_feed.abstract: Political polarization continues to intensify and has inspired substantial research on how individuals’ political identities shape their behaviors as consumers. This stream of research has focused primarily on differences between those on the “left” and the “right” of the political spectrum, offering valuable insights but addressing only one dimension of polarization. The current research introduces the other, currently overlooked dimension, political extremism, and examines how individuals closer to each end of the ideological spectrum differ in post-purchase decision-making from those with weaker or moderate identities. It shows that politically extreme consumers exhibit stronger repurchase likelihood, potentially deriving benefits associated with committing to brands. However, they are also less sensitive to price increases by their chosen brands, even when viable alternatives exist, increasing the risk of overpaying and undermining their financial well-being. These effects are driven by politically extreme consumers’ beliefs in the superiority of their consumption choices and are more pronounced in the presence of threats that originate from the consumption domain (e.g., focal brand product/service failures, competitor new product launches), whereas they diminish in the presence of threats originating from the political domain (e.g., customer–focal brand political misalignment, customer–competitor political alignment).

journal_feed.title: Global Product Strategies and Cultural Promotion in the Context of Culture-Commerce Interactions
journal_feed.abstract: A global firm can strategically maintain or even leverage cultural distance despite it being costless to reduce because such distance fosters consumer cultural adaptation that boosts long-term profits, whereas cultural promotion, though not directly increasing willingness to pay, indirectly enhances profitability by deepening cultural appreciation, ultimately benefiting both the firm and consumers and suggesting that nonprofit cultural initiatives can align with profit-driven goals in global consumerism.

journal_feed.title: The Challenges of Deploying an Algorithmic Pricing Tool: Evidence from Airbnb
journal_feed.abstract: This paper examines the challenges of deploying an AI pricing tool developed by Airbnb and explores possible solutions.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Clarifying Individual Contributions: The Divisibility-Appeal Effect in Fundraising
journal_feed.abstract: Organizers often strategically design numerical information in fundraising campaigns to appeal to contributors with divergent preferences. The current research highlights the importance of jointly considering the goal amount and the requested amount in campaign design, and uncovers a “divisibility-appeal effect,” whereby consumers are more likely to contribute when the campaign’s goal amount is perceived as easily divisible by the requested amount. Seven studies, including ﬁeld, secondary data, and lab experiments, provide convergent evidence for this effect and clarify its underlying mechanism: Fundraising appeals with high (vs. low) divisibility between the goal and requested amount lead to greater perceived clarity of individual contribution toward the fundraising goal, which in turn fosters consumers’ motivation to pursue the collective goal. These findings demonstrate the influence of nuanced numerical signals in collective action contexts and highlight how consumers’ numerical cognition can be effectively utilized in real-world applications to promote the provision of public goods.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Grocery retailers are well-positioned to help address the shortage of EV charging infrastructure but seek insight on the implications for store performance. They lack clarity on the revenue impact of EV charging availability on their parking lots, the underlying mechanisms, and the conditions under which the effect is more pronounced. Drawing on a dataset of over 300 stores of a leading German grocery chain and utilizing a staggered Difference-in-Differences quasi-experimental design, the authors show that EV charging availability increases revenues by 3.4%. Market expansion alone cannot fully explain the effect as the authors find significant evidence for market stealing. They further find that the increase is due to more transactions, not to changes in basket size. The largest increase materializes during off-peak weekend hours. They identify several attitudinal (perceived impulsiveness, storability) and behavioral (penetration, purchase frequency) category characteristics that explain where the revenue increase comes from and provide insights into the role of various store (surface-to-parking ratio, management type) and market (e.g., local competition, apartment-to-house ratio, neighborhood wealth) characteristics. Guidance for store managers interested in increasing the benefits of having EV charging on their premises and chain managers supervising the roll-out throughout their store network is provided.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
journal_feed.abstract: Product performance claims play an important role in shaping consumers’ purchase decisions. Through six preregistered studies, including one field study, the authors demonstrate that consumers’ preferences for point versus range performance estimates in common comparative purchase settings depend on whether their attention is directed toward the content of the claim or the manner of its presentation. At baseline, consumers focus on what information is communicated and prefer point over range estimates because point estimates convey greater certainty about the expected performance outcome. When consumers’ persuasion knowledge is activated, however, their attention shifts toward how information is communicated. In this mode, the format of the claim, rather than the stated performance figures, becomes relatively more informative: range estimates signal brand transparency by acknowledging the natural variability of real-world performance, enhancing perceived trustworthiness and reversing consumer preference. These effects are attenuated when products are evaluated in isolation rather than compared side by side. Collectively, these findings inform both theory and practice by revealing when and why consumers prefer point versus range estimates of product performance.

journal_feed.title: Time-Duration Asymmetries in Consumer Decision-Making
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers routinely make decisions about short time periods, such as waiting for a table or deciding whether to pay for faster delivery. Such periods are often expressed by either a duration or a clock time (e.g., if it is 6:00 PM now, “Your table will be ready in 30 minutes” vs. “Your table will be ready at 6:30 PM”). Eight experiments (N = 16,604) show that these logically equivalent frames change how long a period feels, with downstream consequences for consumer decisions. Relatively short time periods feel longer when framed by duration rather than by start and end time (i.e., clock times or calendar dates), but this pattern reverses as periods get longer. This research refers to this phenomenon as time-duration asymmetry: framing an interval by its start and end time versus its duration changes how long it feels, with the direction of the effect depending on the interval’s length. This research proposes that this occurs because duration frames evoke compressive scalar representations shaped by diminishing sensitivity, whereas start–end frames situate time within structured categorical systems that attenuate compression. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how subtle differences in temporal framing shape perceptions of time and subsequent decisions.

journal_feed.title: Turning Uncertainty into Opportunity: Preference Uncertainty Can Be Beneficial When Consumers Face Outcome Uncertainty
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Consumers can experience two types of uncertainty when purchasing a product. Preference uncertainty (PU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the horizontal product benefits one desires (e.g., “How strong do I want my coffee to be?”). Outcome uncertainty (OU) refers to the uncertainty associated with the actual benefits the product will deliver (e.g., “How strong will the coffee be?”). Ideally, retailers should strive for outcome certainty (i.e., standardize the strength profile of their coffee [coffees in their line]), and help consumers achieve preference certainty (i.e., help consumers learn their ideal coffee strength), so that consumers can purchase the appropriate product with confidence (i.e., achieve a preference-outcome match). Yet there are situations where high OU is a characteristic of the product class, after controlling for quality (e.g., flavor profile of wine). When OU is high, the present research paradoxically finds that high PU leads to more purchase intent than low PU. This effect occurs because people are more optimistic that they will maximize their utility when PU is high (i.e., multiple outcomes could potentially be the best match for their preference) than low (i.e., only one outcome could be the best match for their preference).

journal_feed.title: Frontiers: Discrimination Against Femininity in Headshots: A Field Experiment with AI-Enabled Controllable Stimuli Generation
journal_feed.abstract: Using AI-generated headshots that vary only in femininity, a field experiment finds that consumers discriminate against femininity independently of gender identity.

journal_feed.title: The more, the better? The sustainable additive bias
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract We demonstrate that adding eco-friendly components to offerings improves sustainability judgments, whereas reducing or removing such components—despite potential sustainability gains—receives little recognition. We call this asymmetry the sustainable additive bias . Across nine studies, including a field and a lab experiment, we demonstrate the existence of this bias and uncover its underlying mechanism and boundary conditions. We show that companies are judged more sustainable when they add, rather than subtract, eco-components. This asymmetry is specific to eco-friendly components: consumers recognize the sustainability benefits of removing traditional, less environmentally friendly components. The bias arises because additive changes signal greater environmental effort on the part of the company and is attenuated by prototypicality—that is, the extent to which a component represents a typical example of sustainability. Overall, our findings highlight how environmental cues can distort sustainability judgments and favor additive changes that may be counterproductive to genuine sustainability. We describe the implications of this bias and actions to reduce it.

journal_feed.title: Advice taking across social class: Why (and when) high‐ SES consumers are more likely to take advice from marketplace agents
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract The present research investigates whether consumers of low or high socioeconomic status (SES) are more likely to take advice from marketplace agents. Across five studies (and an additional three in the Methodological Details Appendix), including an analysis of the World Values Survey, and across a range of different advice taking contexts, we find that high‐SES consumers are more likely to take the advice of marketplace agents compared to low‐SES consumers. We demonstrate that this is due to differences in the sources through which high and low‐SES consumers form judgments of trustworthiness, leading high‐SES consumers to perceive advisors as generally more trustworthy, increasing the likelihood that they take their advice. However, these differences are attenuated under two conditions: First, when providing an external trustworthiness cue, differences in advice taking between low‐ and high‐SES consumers are reduced. Second, shifting attention away from the agent and toward one's own product needs and preferences attenuates the effect. This work makes important theoretical contributions regarding how low‐ and high‐SES consumers differ in their propensity to take advice and carries important consumer well‐being implications, particularly for the low‐SES consumer.

journal_feed.title: Navigating Hybrid Logics: Institutional Work in Peer‑to‑Peer Fashion Rental
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
journal_feed.abstract: Building a sustainable wardrobe remains challenging for consumers. Peer‑to‑peer fashion rental (P2PFR) has emerged as an alternative that enables individuals to lend garments for a fee while accessing new styles through temporary use. Based on a qualitative study of consumers’ experiences with P2PFR, this article examines how they navigate the hybrid institutional logics of sustainability and monetization. Our findings identify two strategies through which consumers balance extending clothing use with monetizing their wardrobes: adopting ethical influencer‑style practices and prioritizing brands aligned with their values. These strategies involve substantial institutional work to make garments viable for circulation on digital platforms. This research contributes to consumer research by illuminating how institutional hybridity, and the work it demands, is experienced and enacted in peer‑to‑peer fashion markets, and by offering insights relevant to other platform contexts that similarly seek to profit from prolonging product usability.

journal_feed.title: A dual-LSTM model for CLV distributions: Diverging paths and bimodalities
journal_feed.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Virtually all customer lifetime value (CLV) models reduce the future of a customer to a single number, its expected value, implicitly assuming managers are indifferent to how that value materializes. Yet in a survey of management consultants from a leading global strategy firm, 79% would distinguish between two customers with identical expected CLV but different distributional profiles. This paper argues for a distributional view of CLV and develops a dual-LSTM framework: two interacting long short-term memory networks that jointly predict customer behavior and firm marketing strategy. Because customer responses and firm actions co-evolve dynamically through Monte Carlo simulation, the model generates rich CLV distributions that capture self-fulfilling prophecies, diverging loyalty paths, and bimodal outcomes that traditional approaches cannot structurally anticipate. Calibrated on nine years of individual-level data from 21,939 donors, the dual-LSTM consistently outperforms six benchmarks (including the Pareto/NBD, hierarchical Bayesian extensions, and state-of-the-art deep learning alternatives) on 19 of 24 evaluation metrics. Ranking customers by the right tail of their CLV distribution, rather than by expected CLV, improves targeting lift by up to 8.3%. Most critically, bimodal customers identified by the dual-LSTM—those at a fork in their customer journey—are significantly more responsive to marketing solicitations than observably identical unimodal customers (ROI of an additional solicitation at + 77% vs. -50%), a finding no other benchmark model replicates. These results demonstrate that CLV distributions are both estimable and actionable, enabling firms to allocate resources where marketing interventions yield the greatest marginal impact.

journal_feed.title: Consumer Entrapment
journal_feed.abstract: Abstract Why do consumers sometimes remain trapped in the very practices and communities that once helped them? Consumer practice research has largely emphasized the enabling outcomes of sustained practice participation, with less attention given to how those same practices can become entrapping. This article explores how consumer entrapment emerges within interconnected collective practices. Drawing on an ethnographic study of Chama, a community-based savings and support group in Kenya, it integrates practice theory with Hodder’s theory of entanglement. The study identifies three mechanisms (prefiguration, socialization, and entrenchment) through which participation generates commitments, dependencies, and obligations that produce recurring practice misalignments. Consumers continually work to realign these misalignments, yet under specific conditions, these efforts reproduce the contingencies that sustain participation while progressively deepening entrapment. The findings reveal a central tension: efforts to restore practice alignment can sustain what consumers value while simultaneously reproducing the interdependencies through which consumer entrapment emerges.

journal_feed.title: When and Why Consumers Avoid Purchase on Smartphones
journal_feed.abstract: Consumers increasingly rely on smartphones to browse and compare products, yet they remain substantially less likely to purchase on smartphones than on personal computers (PCs). This research examines the psychological mechanisms underlying this mobile conversion gap, the conditions under which it dissipates, and whether consumer reluctance is warranted. A pilot study, nine controlled experiments, real-world sales analysis, and a field experiment show that smartphone (vs. PC) use reduces purchase likelihood by altering how consumers evaluate their decision process. Specifically, four characteristics of smartphones lead consumers to feel they think less thoroughly when using the device, which then lowers perceived decision quality and reduces purchase likelihood. Consistent with this mechanism, the negative effect of smartphone use on purchase attenuates when decisions are perceived as requiring little thought, whether due to product characteristics, individual differences, or situational contexts, and can be mitigated by interventions that enhance perceived decision quality on smartphones. Importantly, this reluctance is not fully warranted; even when objective performance is equal to or better on smartphones, consumers perceive their decisions more negatively than they do on PCs. The findings reveal a device-specific bias in self-assessment underlying the mobile conversion gap and offer actionable strategies for improving mobile performance.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Effects of Revolving Door Directors on Customer Relationship Performance in Business-to-Government Markets
journal_feed.abstract: Firms in business-to-government (B2G) marketplaces often invite former government officials to join their boards of directors, in search of their critical government connections and knowledge. However, the marketing implications of these revolving door directors are unclear. By analyzing multisource, secondary panel data of 1,731 publicly traded U.S. firms in the B2G market between 2005 and 2021, the authors find that revolving door directors exert significantly positive effects on three dimensions of customer relationship performance: customer acquisition, customer retention, and cross-selling performance. Their government connections and expertise both mediate the effects of revolving door directors on acquisition performance, whereas only government connections mediate the effects on retention and cross-selling performance. The beneficial effects of revolving door directors are contingent on the competitive pressure a firm faces when serving government customers. Specifically, customers’ competitive procurement preference (customer-initiated competition) and exposure to bid protests (competitor-initiated competition) together create procurement uncertainty for sellers in B2G markets, such that revolving door directors are less effective at improving customer relationship performance when customers prefer competitive procurement processes, but more effective when those customers face greater exposure to bid protests.

journal_feed.title: EXPRESS: Every Minute Counts: The Added-Unit Effect In Time Perception
journal_feed.abstract: People encounter and evaluate temporal information every day, for example when evaluating product delivery terms or choosing between online courses. Using data from an online course aggregator platform and nine pre-registered experiments, we show that describing time with a larger and a smaller unit (e.g., “by 8 PM on June 30”, “2 hours and 59 minutes”) rather than with a larger unit alone (e.g., “by the end of day on June 30”, “3 hours”) increases perceived duration. We refer to this phenomenon as the added-unit effect. The added-unit effect emerges because added smaller units change people’s mental representation of time, making them more likely to construe time as a collection of more numerous, smaller units. We document the effect across multiple unit combinations (e.g., dates + hours, hours + minutes, minutes + seconds) and show its implications for online course interest, evaluations of product efficacy, temporal goal setting, and time–money trade-offs. This research contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how number and unit information shape people’s judgments and adds to extant work on time perception.
